children: Latham & Watkins has introduced a new program to reward associates who make meaningful artificial intelligence contributions, the latest in a string of recent moves by law firms to spur AI adoption.

The Los Angeles-founded firm this week said it has set aside $1 million for 2027 to "recognize associates who lead or materially contribute to AI initiatives that create value for clients, practice groups, matter teams or the firm as a whole." Individual awards will vary "based on the significance, impact, and scalability of each contribution," the firm said.

There will be a nomination and review process in the spring to select the award recipients, the firm said. All associates globally are eligible, though the firm did not specify how many people may ultimately split the total pool of money.
Several firms in recent months have invested in ways to promote AI use among associates as the legal industry pushes to incorporate the technology.

Ropes & Gray is among a handful of firms that now allow associates to count time spent gaining AI skills toward their annual billing requirements. First-year associates at the firm can devote up to 20% of their required hours — nearly 400 — to AI, while all associates and counsel can count up to 100 hours.

Ropes & Gray is also including AI as a topic in lawyers' annual review conversations. At A&O Shearman, AI is now a metric in performance evaluations, according to David Wakeling, its global head of AI.

Kirkland & Ellis said in May that it is devoting $500 million ​of its revenue to developing a custom AI platform over the next three to four years. A&O Shearman said earlier this month that it will commit $1.1 billion to its AI strategy over the next five years, with the majority of the planned investment coming from its legal practice teams contributing at least 3% of their time building new tools and services.
Latham has purchased Nvidia servers, leaders at the firm have said, but it has not disclosed the scale of the investment.
